title: Hybrid commitment model for seasonal workloads — PRD draft
body:
Status: draft — exploratory PRD for product + infra alignment.

Summary
------
Problem: many customers have predictable seasonality (weekly spikes, monthly billing cycles, campaign windows). Today they either over-reserve Dedicated capacity year-round (wasteful) or rely heavily on burst which is unpredictable for latency-sensitive inference. We propose a Hybrid Commitment Model (HCM) that blends a small year-round reserved baseline, a seasonal warm-pool of partially committed capacity, and an on-demand burst fabric with soft-isolation rules. The goal is to give customers a lower cost predictable baseline while providing higher confidence for seasonal peaks with clear SLAs and billing semantics.

Goals
-----
- Reduce cost for customers with cyclical demand by enabling short-term seasonal commitments (weekly to quarterly) with discounted rates versus pure on-demand.
- Provide stronger latency guarantees during seasonal peaks by pre-warming and partially locking warm-pool capacity.
- Maintain tenant isolation and fairness: avoid noisy neighbors during seasonal peak windows.
- Keep operations simple to support: automation-first rollout and conservative initial defaults.

Non-goals
---------
- Not a full replacement for Reserved Capacity contracts (annual/enterprise). HCM targets teams that cannot or will not commit a full annual reservation.
- Not intended as a general marketplace for arbitrary capacity trading between customers in year one.

Background and motivation
-------------------------
- Customer interviews (sales + CS) surfaced many use-cases: seasonal ad-campaigns, weekly data processing windows, holiday traffic surges for ecommerce, and month-end batch evaluation workloads.
- Current product options: 1) year-long reserved blocks (Dedicated) — predictable but high upfront cost; 2) burst-on-demand — cheap but subject to preemption/latency variability.
- Operators: bursts result in complex fallbacks and higher support tickets when predictions fail.

High-level model
----------------
1) Baseline Reserve: a small committed pool (e.g., 20–50% of average steady-state) billed monthly.
2) Seasonal Commitment: customers can request a time-bounded seasonal commit (1 week — 3 months). Seasonal commit purchases discounted units that are placed into a Warm Pool for the duration. These units are pre-warmed and instrumented for rapid allocation.
3) Burst/Overflow Fabric: uncommitted on-demand nodes that can be used when seasonal and baseline capacity are saturated. Burst has lower latency guarantees and can be preemptible depending on tenant tier.

Key primitives and semantics
---------------------------
- Warm Pool Allocation: units in seasonal commit are kept in a pre-warmed state (model weights loaded, KV cache primed for canonical prompts if provided). Warm Pool reduces cold-start token-latency.
- Soft-commit vs Hard-commit: seasonal units can be soft-commit (can be reclaimed under extreme cluster pressure with 5–15s drain) or hard-commit (guaranteed for the window with SLA uplift). Price varies accordingly.
- Credit decay + rollover: unused seasonal units convert to credits at a reduced rate with a short decay window (e.g., up to 2 weeks) to avoid over-provisioning claims.
- Tenant QoS Lanes: isolation achieved by mapping seasonal commitments to QoS lanes with admission control and backpressure policies.

Allocation algorithm (sketch)
----------------------------
Inputs: historical load (p95), campaign schedule (customer supplied), current cluster headroom, predicted fleet availability.
Outputs: warm-pool sizing recommendation, soft/hard split, expected cost delta vs baseline.
Algorithm steps (high-level):
- Fit seasonality model (Fourier + recent trends) on hourly token throughput for last N months.
- Detect campaign windows (customer annotated or heuristics) and estimate peak delta.
- Compute minimal warm-pool units to meet customer's target p99 latency under predicted peak given batching policies.
- Factor in model cold-start distributions to decide what fraction must be hard-commit.
- Recommend a season commitment size + billing tier with simulation of regret (cost vs on-demand).

Isolation controls
------------------
- QoS Lanes: each seasonal commit maps to a QoS lane with token-level backpressure thresholds and tenant-weighted fair-shares.
- Tenant sandboxing: warm pool instances tied to tenant-specific placement constraints (no co-locating heavy noisy tenants on same host).
- Eviction policy: soft-commit units evicted only after exhausting burst alternatives and with customer notification hooks. Hard-commit units require operator sign-off for forced reclamation.
- Graceful degradation: traffic overage routed into a degrade policy chain (model-quantized surrogate, lower batch sizes, or fallback model) before eviction.

Autoscaling and triggers
------------------------
- Autoscaler uses a two-tier signal: baseline autoscale for steady-state, and seasonal autoscale augmenter during declared windows.
- Triggers: token queue latency, pending request burst count, temperature of KV cache misses, and host readiness.
- Pre-warm triggers: N hours before campaign start (customer-configurable) trigger pre-warm snapshot load.

Pricing and billing implications
------------------------------
- Hybrid pricing: baseline monthly rate + seasonal commit fees (time-bounded) with optional hard-commit premium.
- Credits: partial refunds as credits when seasonal commit not used; credits decay to avoid accounting complexity.
- Marketplace concerns: recommend starting as a direct contract add-on, not a public marketplace feature.

Operator/Infra impacts
----------------------
- Warm-pool lifecycle management: new resource controller for warm instances, snapshotting model state and KV priming APIs.
- Scheduler changes: QoS lanes and tenant anti-affinity annotations.
- Telemetry: new metrics — warm-pool utilization, pre-warm success rate, seasonal SLA breaches, credit conversion rate.

Observability and SLOs
---------------------
- New SLOs for seasonal commits: 99th-token-latency during committed windows (separate for hard vs soft).
- Dashboard: per-tenant seasonal timeline, utilization heatmap, and predicted vs actual peak.
- Alerts: when warm-pool shortfall predicted < 6 hours before campaign start.

Rollout plan (phased)
---------------------
Phase 0 — experiment (Q1): surface recommendations and simulated costs in Console, no billing change. Invite 5 pilot customers.
Phase 1 — soft-commit GA (Q2): enable seasonal soft-commit contracts with conservative defaults (max 2-week windows).
Phase 2 — hard-commit + SLA (Q3): introduce hard-commit upgrade and corresponding SLA + billing flows.
Phase 3 — automation + self-serve (Q4): Console flows for purchase, scheduling, and pre-warm configuration.

Runbook highlights
------------------
- If warm-pool underprovisioned during campaign start: 1) auto-escalate to burst fabric with VIP routing, 2) notify customer and recommend degrade policies, 3) if sustained, trigger emergency reallocation with operator approval.
- Incident playbook entry points: warm-pool OOM, pre-warm failure, credit reconciliation mismatch.

Acceptance criteria (for Phase 1)
--------------------------------
- Pilot customers see median cost reduction >=10% vs continuous reserved baseline for seasonal workloads.
- 95% of declared campaign starts meet the p99 latency target with warm-pool + burst fallback.
- No more than 2 Sev1 incidents caused by warm-pool allocation in pilot cohort across 3 months.

Open questions / risks
---------------------
- Accounting complexity vs customer value: how generous should credit conversion be?
- Competitive positioning: will this cannibalize Reserved contracts? (mitigation: higher hard-commit premium).
- Ops complexity: scheduler and infra changes could be non-trivial.
- Security/compliance: any tenancy mixing in warm pool may violate some enterprise policies — need private deploy guardrails.

Next steps (immediate)
----------------------
- Product + infra sync: DED-4312 (epic) to align on scheduler API changes.
- Identify 3 pilot customers via AE/CS with predictable seasonality.
- Prototype warm-pool controller and pre-warm API in serving-runtime repo (PR linked above).
- Design billing contract language with finance/legal for pilot.

Notes to self / rough ideas
--------------------------
- Consider offering a campaign template in Console (preset pre-warm lead times based on historical data).
- Could integrate with Optimize: recommend warm-pool size automatically based on cost vs qps.
- Experiment: allow customers to donate unused seasonal units to open pool in exchange for deeper discounts (longer term idea).
